subject: Business
title: Survivorship Bias: The Silent Failures
description: A quick win: understand Survivorship Bias: The Silent Failures.

hook.text: In WWII, engineers studied bullet holes on returning planes. Abraham Wald said: armor the places with no holes.

buildup.text: Survivorship bias means we study successes and ignore the failures we never see.

discovery.text: The planes with holes in those other spots never came back. The data was missing, not absent.

twist.text: Business books study successful founders, ignoring thousands who did the same things and failed.

climax.text: Steve Jobs dropped out of college and succeeded. Millions dropped out and you'll never hear of them.

punchline.text: Don't copy survivors. Study what killed everyone else.

quiz.question: What did Abraham Wald recommend about the planes?
options: Armor the areas without bullet holes — those planes didn't survive
Remove armor to make planes lighter

details.summary: Survivorship bias occurs when analysis focuses only on successful examples while ignoring failures that did not survive to be studied. Business advice drawn only from successful companies can be dangerously misleading because it misses the failed companies that did the same things.
details.whyItMatters: Survivorship bias produces false lessons from success stories. A strategy that appears common among winners may be equally common among failures. Studying both survivors and failures is essential for valid business insights.
takeaways: Studying only successes produces misleading conclusions about what works
Failed examples are often invisible, creating a skewed sample
Abraham Wald's WWII bomber analysis is the classic survivorship bias example

faq.question: How does survivorship bias distort business advice?
faq.answer: Books studying successful companies identify common traits and present them as success recipes. But failed companies often shared those same traits. Without examining failures, you cannot determine whether a trait actually contributes to success or is merely common across all companies.

faq.question: What is the Abraham Wald bomber analysis story?
faq.answer: In WWII, the military planned to add armor where returning bombers had bullet holes. Wald realized they should armor where returning bombers had no holes because planes hit in those areas did not return. The surviving planes created a biased sample of non-fatal damage.
